title: Chocolate Chip Cookies
subtitle: Soft and chewy with crisp edges
excerpt: Brown butter, two types of sugar, and an extra yolk give these cookies a rich caramel depth. The edges crisp while the centres stay chewy. Best eaten warm from the oven.

recipe.sourceNotes: The chocolate chip cookie was invented by Ruth Wakefield at the Toll House Inn in Massachusetts in 1938. The original Toll House recipe used all-purpose flour, shortening, and two types of sugar. Later refinements from American bakers including Jacques Torres and David Leite established that browning the butter, chilling the dough, and using an extra yolk produce a chewier, more complex result. The British adaptation uses plain flour and a mix of caster and soft brown sugar.

content.text: Brown the butter before mixing: it adds a nutty, caramel flavour that makes a significant difference. The dough will look very soft when scooped, but it firms up as it bakes. Pull the cookies from the oven when the edges are set but the centres still look underdone: they continue to cook on the hot tray. Do not skip the resting time on the tray.

Melt the butter in a saucepan over medium heat. Continue cooking, swirling occasionally, until the butter turns golden and smells nutty, about 3 to 4 minutes. Pour into a large bowl and leave to cool for 10 minutes.
Heat the oven to 180 C / fan 160 C / gas 4. Line two baking trays with baking paper.
Whisk both sugars into the brown butter until well combined. Add the whole egg, extra yolk, and vanilla extract. Whisk vigorously for 1 minute until the mixture is smooth and slightly thickened.
Fold in the flour, bicarbonate of soda, and salt until just combined. Stir in the chocolate chips.
Scoop heaped tablespoons of dough onto the lined trays, leaving 5 cm between each. Bake for 10 to 12 minutes until the edges are set and golden but the centres still look slightly underdone.
Leave on the tray for 5 minutes before transferring to a rack. The cookies will firm up as they cool.
